description: Comprehensive question bank derived from Earthquakes chapter covering seismic waves, measurement, India and Karnataka seismic zones, tsunamis and preparedness. All syllabus points covered without duplication.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is an earthquake?

options.A: A gradual sinking of the Earth's crust
options.B: The sudden shaking of the Earth's surface caused by the rapid release of energy within the Earth
options.C: A type of volcanic eruption
options.D: A large ocean wave generated by wind

questions.explanation: An earthquake is the sudden shaking of the Earth's surface caused by the rapid release of energy within the Earth. The most common cause is sudden slip along a fault after stress has accumulated in rocks.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the scientific study of earthquakes called?

options.A: Geology
options.B: Seismology
options.C: Volcanology
options.D: Oceanography

questions.explanation: Seismology is the scientific study of earthquakes and the generation, propagation and recording of seismic waves.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What causes most earthquakes?

options.A: Volcanic eruptions
options.B: Meteorite impacts
options.C: Tectonic movement of lithospheric plates causing stress accumulation along faults
options.D: Ocean tides

questions.explanation: Most earthquakes are tectonic. Movement of lithospheric plates causes stress to accumulate along faults. When frictional resistance is overcome, rocks suddenly slip and release stored elastic strain energy as seismic waves.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is elastic rebound theory?

options.A: Theory that rocks bounce back after an earthquake due to gravity
options.B: Theory that rocks on either side of a locked fault gradually deform as tectonic stress builds, and when the fault ruptures, the rocks spring partly back towards an undeformed state, releasing stored energy
options.C: Theory that earthquakes are caused by elastic waves in the ocean
options.D: Theory that the Earth's crust rebounds after volcanic activity

questions.explanation: Elastic rebound theory explains that rocks on either side of a locked fault gradually deform as tectonic stress builds. When the fault ruptures, the rocks spring partly back towards an undeformed state, releasing stored energy and generating an earthquake.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a fault?

options.A: A type of seismic wave
options.B: A fracture or zone of fractures in rock along which displacement has occurred
options.C: The point on the surface above an earthquake
options.D: An instrument that records earthquakes

questions.explanation: A fault is a fracture or zone of fractures in rock along which displacement has occurred. Earthquakes commonly occur when blocks of rock suddenly move along faults.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which type of earthquake results from fault movement associated with plate tectonics?

options.A: Volcanic earthquake
options.B: Collapse earthquake
options.C: Tectonic earthquake
options.D: Induced earthquake

questions.explanation: Tectonic earthquakes result from fault movement associated with plate tectonics. They are especially common near plate boundaries but can also occur within plates along older or reactivated faults.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a volcanic earthquake?

options.A: An earthquake caused by sudden fault slip due to tectonic stress
options.B: Seismic activity associated with magma movement, fracturing of rocks and pressure changes in a volcanic system
options.C: An earthquake caused by underground mine collapse
options.D: An earthquake triggered by reservoir impoundment

questions.explanation: A volcanic earthquake is seismic activity associated with magma movement, fracturing of rocks and pressure changes in a volcanic system. It may occur before or during an eruption, but not every volcanic earthquake leads to an eruption.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is an induced earthquake?

options.A: An earthquake caused by plate boundary movement
options.B: An earthquake triggered or influenced by human activities that alter stress or pore-fluid pressure in the Earth's crust
options.C: An earthquake that occurs before a larger earthquake
options.D: An earthquake that occurs deep within the Earth

questions.explanation: An induced earthquake is triggered or influenced by human activities that alter stress or pore-fluid pressure in the Earth's crust. Examples include some reservoir-induced events, mining-related seismicity and earthquakes associated with deep fluid injection.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Are all earthquakes caused by plate boundaries?

options.A: Yes, all earthquakes occur at plate boundaries
options.B: No, many occur within plates along ancient faults or zones of weakness, and human-induced and volcanic earthquakes also occur
options.C: Yes, except volcanic earthquakes
options.D: No, only induced earthquakes occur away from plate boundaries

questions.explanation: No. Many earthquakes occur within plates along ancient faults or zones of weakness. Human-induced and volcanic earthquakes also occur.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a collapse earthquake?

options.A: An earthquake caused by plate movement
options.B: An earthquake that may occur when underground cavities or mines collapse
options.C: An earthquake caused by volcanic activity
options.D: An earthquake caused by meteorite impact

questions.explanation: Collapse earthquakes may occur when underground cavities or mines collapse.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which factors influence the damage caused by an earthquake?

options.A: Only magnitude
options.B: Only depth and distance
options.C: Magnitude, depth, distance from the source, duration and frequency content of shaking, local soil and geological conditions, building design and construction quality, population density, time of occurrence and preparedness
options.D: Only building design

questions.explanation: Magnitude, depth, distance from the source, duration and frequency content of shaking, local soil and geological conditions, building design and construction quality, population density, time of occurrence and preparedness all influence damage.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the focus of an earthquake?

options.A: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the earthquake
options.B: The point inside the Earth where the rupture begins and seismic energy is first released
options.C: The depth of the earthquake below the surface
options.D: The area of maximum damage

questions.explanation: The focus, also called the hypocentre, is the point inside the Earth where the rupture begins and seismic energy is first released.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?

options.A: The point inside the Earth where the rupture begins
options.B: The point on the Earth's surface vertically above the earthquake focus
options.C: The depth of the earthquake below the surface
options.D: The area of minimum damage

questions.explanation: The epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface vertically above the earthquake focus.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is focal depth?

options.A: The depth of the epicentre below the surface
options.B: The vertical distance from the Earth's surface to the earthquake focus
options.C: The horizontal distance from the epicentre to the fault
options.D: The depth of the Earth's crust

questions.explanation: Focal depth is the vertical distance from the Earth's surface to the earthquake focus.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How are earthquakes classified by focal depth?

options.A: Shallow-focus (0-70 km), intermediate-focus (70-300 km), and deep-focus (300-700 km)
options.B: Shallow-focus (0-50 km), intermediate-focus (50-200 km), and deep-focus (200-500 km)
options.C: Shallow-focus (0-100 km), intermediate-focus (100-400 km), and deep-focus (400-800 km)
options.D: Shallow-focus (0-30 km), intermediate-focus (30-150 km), and deep-focus (150-600 km)

questions.explanation: A common broad classification is shallow-focus earthquakes (0-70 km), intermediate-focus earthquakes (70-300 km) and deep-focus earthquakes (300-700 km). Boundaries are approximate and conventions may vary slightly.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why are shallow earthquakes often more damaging?

options.A: They have higher magnitude
options.B: When other factors are similar, a shallow earthquake generally releases energy closer to the surface, so strong shaking may occur near the source
options.C: They last longer than deep earthquakes
options.D: They always occur in populated areas

questions.explanation: When other factors are similar, a shallow earthquake generally releases energy closer to the surface, so strong shaking may occur near the source. Actual damage still depends on magnitude, geology, buildings and distance.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can the epicentre be the place of maximum damage?

options.A: Yes, the epicentre is always the place of maximum damage
options.B: No, the epicentre never experiences maximum damage
options.C: It may be near the area of strongest shaking, but not necessarily; local soil amplification, rupture direction, depth, building vulnerability and other factors can cause maximum damage away from the epicentre
options.D: Only for deep earthquakes

questions.explanation: The epicentre may be near the area of strongest shaking, but not necessarily. Local soil amplification, rupture direction, depth, building vulnerability and other factors can cause maximum damage away from the epicentre.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is an aftershock?

options.A: A smaller or subsequent earthquake following a larger event in the same affected region
options.B: An earthquake that precedes a larger earthquake
options.C: The point inside the Earth where rupture starts
options.D: A surface point above the focus

questions.explanation: An aftershock is a smaller or subsequent earthquake following a larger event in the same affected region.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a foreshock?

options.A: A smaller earthquake following a larger event
options.B: An earthquake that precedes a larger earthquake in the same region; identified as a foreshock only in retrospect
options.C: An earthquake caused by volcanic activity
options.D: An earthquake that occurs deep underground

questions.explanation: A foreshock is an earthquake that precedes a larger earthquake in the same region; it is identified as a foreshock only in retrospect.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are seismic waves?

options.A: Waves on the ocean surface caused by earthquakes
options.B: Waves of energy generated by an earthquake or other source and transmitted through the Earth or along its surface
options.C: Sound waves produced by volcanic eruptions
options.D: Electromagnetic waves from the Earth's core

questions.explanation: Seismic waves are waves of energy generated by an earthquake or other source and transmitted through the Earth or along its surface. They are recorded by seismological instruments.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are the two broad groups of seismic waves?

options.A: P-waves and S-waves
options.B: Body waves and surface waves
options.C: Love waves and Rayleigh waves
options.D: Compressional waves and shear waves

questions.explanation: Body waves, which travel through Earth's interior, and surface waves, which travel along or near Earth's surface.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which waves are body waves?

options.A: Love waves and Rayleigh waves
options.B: Primary waves (P-waves) and secondary waves (S-waves)
options.C: Surface waves and tidal waves
options.D: Compressional waves and surface waves

questions.explanation: Primary waves (P-waves) and secondary waves (S-waves) are body waves.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which waves are surface waves?

options.A: P-waves and S-waves
options.B: Love waves and Rayleigh waves
options.C: Compressional waves and shear waves
options.D: Body waves and primary waves

questions.explanation: The principal types of surface waves are Love waves and Rayleigh waves. They travel along the Earth's surface and often cause strong, damaging ground motion.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are P-waves?

options.A: Secondary or shear seismic waves
options.B: Primary or compressional seismic waves; the fastest seismic body waves generally recorded first by a seismograph
options.C: Surface waves that produce rolling motion
options.D: Waves that travel only through liquids

questions.explanation: P-waves are primary or compressional seismic waves. They are the fastest seismic body waves and are generally recorded first by a seismograph.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How do P-waves travel?

options.A: Particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation
options.B: Particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction in which the wave travels, producing alternating compression and expansion
options.C: Particles move in a rolling elliptical motion
options.D: Particles move side-to-side horizontally

questions.explanation: In P-waves, particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction in which the wave travels, producing alternating compression and expansion.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can P-waves travel through solids, liquids and gases?

options.A: Only through solids
options.B: Only through solids and liquids
options.C: Yes, P-waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases, although their speeds vary with the material
options.D: Only through gases

questions.explanation: Yes. P-waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases, although their speeds vary with the material.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why are P-waves called primary waves?

options.A: They are the most important waves
options.B: They are usually the first seismic waves to reach a recording station because they travel faster than S-waves and surface waves
options.C: They are the only waves that cause damage
options.D: They originate first in the Earth's core

questions.explanation: They are usually the first seismic waves to reach a recording station because they travel faster than S-waves and surface waves.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are S-waves?

options.A: Primary or compressional seismic waves
options.B: Secondary or shear seismic waves; slower than P-waves and generally arrive second at a recording station
options.C: Surface waves that produce rolling motion
options.D: Waves that travel through all mediums

questions.explanation: S-waves are secondary or shear seismic waves. They are slower than P-waves and generally arrive second at a recording station.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How do S-waves travel?

options.A: Particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation
options.B: Particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation, producing shear deformation
options.C: Particles move in a rolling elliptical motion
options.D: Particles move back and forth producing compression

questions.explanation: In S-waves, particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. They produce shear deformation.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can S-waves travel through liquids?

options.A: Yes, S-waves can travel through all mediums
options.B: No, S-waves cannot propagate through liquids because liquids do not support the shear rigidity required for shear waves
options.C: Yes, but only through very viscous liquids
options.D: Only through gases

questions.explanation: No. S-waves cannot propagate through liquids because liquids do not support the shear rigidity required for shear waves. Their absence through Earth's liquid outer core is important evidence that the outer core is liquid.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why are S-waves important in understanding Earth's interior?

options.A: They are the fastest waves
options.B: Their inability to travel through liquids helps scientists infer the liquid state of the outer core; changes in seismic-wave speeds and paths also reveal internal boundaries and material properties
options.C: They cause the most damage
options.D: They are the only waves that travel through the core

questions.explanation: Their inability to travel through liquids helps scientists infer the liquid state of the outer core. Changes in seismic-wave speeds and paths also reveal internal boundaries and material properties.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are surface waves?

options.A: Waves that travel through Earth's interior
options.B: Waves that travel along the Earth's surface or near-surface layers; generally slower than body waves but can produce large-amplitude shaking and substantial damage
options.C: Waves that travel only through the core
options.D: Waves that are the fastest seismic waves

questions.explanation: Surface waves travel along the Earth's surface or near-surface layers. They are generally slower than body waves but can produce large-amplitude shaking and substantial damage.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are Love waves?

options.A: Body waves that travel through the interior
options.B: Surface waves that produce mainly horizontal side-to-side shear motion, generally perpendicular to the direction of propagation, without vertical rolling motion
options.C: Surface waves that produce rolling elliptical motion
options.D: Compressional waves that travel fastest

questions.explanation: Love waves produce mainly horizontal side-to-side shear motion, generally perpendicular to the direction of propagation, without the vertical rolling motion characteristic of Rayleigh waves.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are Rayleigh waves?

options.A: Body waves that travel through solids only
options.B: Surface waves that produce a rolling, elliptical particle motion that includes both vertical and horizontal components, similar in broad appearance to ocean waves
options.C: Surface waves that produce only horizontal side-to-side motion
options.D: Primary waves that travel fastest

questions.explanation: Rayleigh waves produce a rolling, elliptical particle motion that includes both vertical and horizontal components, similar in broad appearance to ocean waves.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why can surface waves be highly destructive?

options.A: They travel through the Earth's core
options.B: They often have large amplitudes and can produce prolonged horizontal and vertical ground motion near the surface, which may strongly affect buildings, bridges and other structures
options.C: They are the fastest seismic waves
options.D: They only occur in coastal areas

questions.explanation: They often have large amplitudes and can produce prolonged horizontal and vertical ground motion near the surface, which may strongly affect buildings, bridges and other structures.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a seismograph?

options.A: The recorded trace of ground motion
options.B: An instrument or recording system used to detect and record ground motion caused by earthquakes and other vibrations
options.C: The point inside the Earth where rupture begins
options.D: A scale used to measure earthquake intensity

questions.explanation: A seismograph is an instrument or recording system used to detect and record ground motion caused by earthquakes and other vibrations.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a seismometer?

options.A: The recorded trace of ground motion
options.B: The sensor that measures ground motion; in common usage, seismograph may refer to the complete instrument and recording system, while seismometer refers more specifically to the sensing component
options.C: A scale used to measure earthquake magnitude
options.D: An instrument that predicts earthquakes

questions.explanation: A seismometer is the sensor that measures ground motion. In common usage, seismograph may refer to the complete instrument and recording system, while seismometer refers more specifically to the sensing component.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a seismogram?

options.A: An instrument that records earthquakes
options.B: The recorded trace or digital record of ground motion produced by a seismograph
options.C: The point inside the Earth where rupture begins
options.D: A scale used to measure earthquake intensity

questions.explanation: A seismogram is the recorded trace or digital record of ground motion produced by a seismograph.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does a traditional seismograph work?

options.A: It uses GPS to detect ground movement
options.B: A suspended mass tends to remain relatively stationary due to inertia while the instrument frame moves with the ground; the relative motion is measured and recorded. Modern instruments use electronic sensors and digital data acquisition
options.C: It measures the temperature changes caused by earthquakes
options.D: It uses sound waves to detect earthquakes

questions.explanation: A suspended mass tends to remain relatively stationary due to inertia while the instrument frame moves with the ground. The relative motion is measured and recorded. Modern instruments use electronic sensors and digital data acquisition.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How are earthquakes located using seismograms?

options.A: By measuring the surface waves only
options.B: The time difference between P-wave and S-wave arrivals is used to estimate the distance from a station to the earthquake; data from at least three suitably placed stations can be used for triangulation to estimate the epicentre
options.C: By measuring the temperature at the epicentre
options.D: By using satellite images

questions.explanation: The time difference between P-wave and S-wave arrivals is used to estimate the distance from a station to the earthquake. Data from at least three suitably placed stations can be used for triangulation to estimate the epicentre.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can a seismograph measure earthquake magnitude directly?

options.A: Yes, a seismograph directly measures magnitude
options.B: A seismograph records ground motion; magnitude is calculated from recorded wave amplitudes and other parameters, with corrections for distance, frequency, instrument response and, depending on the scale, seismic moment
options.C: No, seismographs cannot record ground motion
options.D: Only digital seismographs can measure magnitude

questions.explanation: A seismograph records ground motion. Magnitude is calculated from recorded wave amplitudes and other parameters, with corrections for distance, frequency, instrument response and, depending on the scale, seismic moment.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is earthquake magnitude?

options.A: The observed strength of shaking and its effects at a particular location
options.B: A quantitative measure of the size of an earthquake at its source, expressed as a single value for an event
options.C: The depth of the earthquake below the surface
options.D: The amount of damage caused by an earthquake

questions.explanation: Magnitude is a quantitative measure of the size of an earthquake at its source. It is expressed as a single value for an event, although different magnitude scales may produce slightly different values.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is earthquake intensity?

options.A: The size of the earthquake at its source
options.B: The observed strength of shaking and its effects at a particular location, including how people feel it and the damage to buildings and the environment
options.C: The depth of the earthquake focus
options.D: The speed of seismic waves

questions.explanation: Intensity describes the observed strength of shaking and its effects at a particular location, including how people feel it and the damage to buildings and the environment. It can vary from place to place for the same earthquake.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the difference between magnitude and intensity?

options.A: Magnitude describes local effects; intensity estimates the size of the earthquake source
options.B: Magnitude estimates the size of the earthquake source; intensity describes the local effects of shaking at a site. One earthquake has one principal magnitude estimate but can have many intensity values across the affected region
options.C: Both measure the same thing
options.D: Magnitude varies from place to place; intensity is a single value

questions.explanation: Magnitude estimates the size of the earthquake source; intensity describes the local effects of shaking at a site. One earthquake has one principal magnitude estimate but can have many intensity values across the affected region.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Richter scale?

options.A: A scale that measures the observed effects of shaking at a location
options.B: The common name for the local magnitude scale (ML), developed by Charles F. Richter in 1935 to quantify the size of relatively nearby earthquakes in southern California using recorded seismic-wave amplitudes
options.C: A scale based on seismic moment
options.D: A scale that measures tsunami height

questions.explanation: The Richter scale is the common name for the local magnitude scale (ML), developed by Charles F. Richter in 1935 to quantify the size of relatively nearby earthquakes in southern California using recorded seismic-wave amplitudes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Is the Richter scale linear?

options.A: Yes, it is a linear scale
options.B: No, it is logarithmic; a one-unit increase corresponds to ten times the recorded wave amplitude under the scale's defined conditions
options.C: It is a logarithmic scale but a one-unit increase means two times amplitude
options.D: It is a linear scale for small earthquakes only

questions.explanation: No. It is logarithmic. A one-unit increase corresponds to ten times the recorded wave amplitude under the scale's defined conditions. The energy released increases by roughly 32 times for each whole-number magnitude step as a useful approximation.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Is the Richter scale suitable for all very large earthquakes?

options.A: Yes, it works for all earthquake sizes
options.B: No, the original local magnitude scale can saturate for large earthquakes and is not ideal for very large or distant events; modern reporting generally favours moment magnitude for large earthquakes
options.C: Yes, but only for deep earthquakes
options.D: No, it only works for volcanic earthquakes

questions.explanation: No. The original local magnitude scale can saturate for large earthquakes and is not ideal for very large or distant events. Modern reporting generally favours moment magnitude for large earthquakes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does a magnitude 6 earthquake release ten times the energy of a magnitude 5 earthquake?

options.A: Yes, energy increases ten times per unit
options.B: No, the recorded wave amplitude is about ten times greater for a one-unit increase, while the energy release is approximately 32 times greater
options.C: Yes, both amplitude and energy increase ten times
options.D: No, energy increases only two times per unit

questions.explanation: No. The recorded wave amplitude is about ten times greater for a one-unit increase, while the energy release is approximately 32 times greater.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the moment magnitude scale?

options.A: A scale that measures observed shaking and damage at a location
options.B: A logarithmic magnitude scale based on seismic moment, which reflects the rigidity of rocks, the area of the fault that slipped and the average amount of slip
options.C: A scale developed by Charles Richter in 1935
options.D: A scale that measures tsunami run-up

questions.explanation: Moment magnitude (Mw) is a logarithmic magnitude scale based on seismic moment, which reflects the rigidity of rocks, the area of the fault that slipped and the average amount of slip.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why is moment magnitude preferred for large earthquakes?

options.A: It is easier to calculate than the Richter scale
options.B: It is physically related to the size of the earthquake source and does not saturate in the same way as older magnitude scales for very large events; it provides a consistent measure across a wide range of earthquake sizes
options.C: It measures intensity directly
options.D: It was developed before the Richter scale

questions.explanation: It is physically related to the size of the earthquake source and does not saturate in the same way as older magnitude scales for very large events. It provides a consistent measure across a wide range of earthquake sizes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is seismic moment?

options.A: The observed damage at a location
options.B: A measure of the physical size of an earthquake source, calculated from the rigidity of the rocks, the area of the fault rupture and the average displacement along the fault
options.C: The time difference between P-wave and S-wave arrivals
options.D: The depth of the earthquake focus

questions.explanation: Seismic moment is a measure of the physical size of an earthquake source. It is calculated from the rigidity of the rocks, the area of the fault rupture and the average displacement along the fault.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Who developed the moment magnitude scale?

options.A: Charles F. Richter
options.B: Thomas C. Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori in 1979
options.C: Giuseppe Mercalli
options.D: John Milne

questions.explanation: Thomas C. Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori introduced the moment magnitude scale in 1979.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Mercalli intensity scale?

options.A: A scale based on seismic moment
options.B: The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale describes the effects of earthquake shaking at a particular location, based on human observations, effects on objects, and damage to structures
options.C: A scale that measures the size of the earthquake source
options.D: A scale that measures tsunami wave height

questions.explanation: The Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale describes the effects of earthquake shaking at a particular location, based on human observations, effects on objects, and damage to structures.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How many levels are in the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale?

options.A: 10 levels, from I to X
options.B: 12 levels, from I to XII
options.C: 8 levels, from I to VIII
options.D: 15 levels, from I to XV

questions.explanation: It has 12 levels, from I (not felt or felt by very few) to XII (total or near-total destruction in the traditional description).

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does Mercalli intensity measure energy released at the focus?

options.A: Yes, it measures the total energy released
options.B: No, it describes the observed effects and shaking at a location, not the total energy released at the earthquake source
options.C: Yes, but only for shallow earthquakes
options.D: It measures both energy and effects

questions.explanation: No. It describes the observed effects and shaking at a location, not the total energy released at the earthquake source.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why can the same earthquake have different Mercalli intensities?

options.A: Because the magnitude changes from place to place
options.B: Because shaking varies with distance from the source, depth, local geology, soil conditions, topography and building vulnerability
options.C: Because the focus moves during the earthquake
options.D: Because the scale is not standardized

questions.explanation: Shaking varies with distance from the source, depth, local geology, soil conditions, topography and building vulnerability. Therefore, intensity differs across locations.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What does MMI level I indicate?

options.A: Total destruction
options.B: Not felt except by very few under especially favourable conditions
options.C: Severe shaking with considerable damage
options.D: Moderate shaking felt by all

questions.explanation: MMI level I indicates not felt except by very few under especially favourable conditions.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What does MMI level XII indicate?

options.A: Not felt
options.B: Weak shaking felt by some people
options.C: Total or near-total destruction in the traditional description
options.D: Light shaking with no damage

questions.explanation: MMI level XII indicates total or near-total destruction in the traditional description.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What do MMI levels II-III generally indicate?

options.A: Extreme to catastrophic effects
options.B: Weak shaking; felt by some people, especially indoors
options.C: Severe to violent shaking
options.D: Total destruction

questions.explanation: MMI levels II-III indicate weak shaking; felt by some people, especially indoors.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What do MMI levels IV-V generally indicate?

options.A: Not felt
options.B: Light to moderate shaking; noticeable movement of objects
options.C: Total destruction
options.D: Extreme damage

questions.explanation: MMI levels IV-V indicate light to moderate shaking; noticeable movement of objects.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What do MMI levels VI-VII generally indicate?

options.A: Weak shaking felt indoors
options.B: Strong to very strong shaking; slight to moderate damage may occur
options.C: Extreme to catastrophic effects
options.D: Not felt at all

questions.explanation: MMI levels VI-VII indicate strong to very strong shaking; slight to moderate damage may occur.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What do MMI levels VIII-IX generally indicate?

options.A: Light shaking
options.B: Severe to violent shaking; considerable damage in vulnerable structures
options.C: No damage
options.D: Weak shaking felt by few

questions.explanation: MMI levels VIII-IX indicate severe to violent shaking; considerable damage in vulnerable structures.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What do MMI levels X-XII generally indicate?

options.A: Weak shaking
options.B: Extreme to catastrophic effects; very severe damage and major changes to the built or natural environment
options.C: Light to moderate shaking
options.D: Moderate damage only

questions.explanation: MMI levels X-XII indicate extreme to catastrophic effects; very severe damage and major changes to the built or natural environment.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is seismic zoning?

options.A: The process of predicting earthquakes
options.B: Dividing a region into areas according to expected levels of earthquake ground shaking or seismic hazard for planning and engineering purposes
options.C: The measurement of earthquake magnitude
options.D: The study of seismic waves

questions.explanation: Seismic zoning divides a region into areas according to expected levels of earthquake ground shaking or seismic hazard for planning and engineering purposes. It helps guide earthquake-resistant construction and risk reduction.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How many seismic zones are used in India's current commonly cited BIS zoning framework?

options.A: Three zones: II, III, IV
options.B: Four zones: II, III, IV and V; Zone I is not used in this current four-zone classification
options.C: Five zones: I, II, III, IV, V
options.D: Six zones

questions.explanation: The BIS seismic zoning framework in IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016 classifies India into four zones: Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV and Zone V. Zone I is not used in this current four-zone classification.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which is the most earthquake-prone seismic zone in India's four-zone classification?

options.A: Zone II
options.B: Zone III
options.C: Zone IV
options.D: Zone V

questions.explanation: Zone V is the highest seismic-hazard zone in the four-zone classification.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which is the least severe seismic zone in India's four-zone classification?

options.A: Zone II
options.B: Zone III
options.C: Zone IV
options.D: Zone V

questions.explanation: Zone II is the lowest seismic-hazard zone in the four-zone classification; it does not mean that earthquakes are impossible there.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which parts of India are broadly associated with Zone V?

options.A: Only the Deccan Plateau
options.B: Much of the northeastern region, parts of the Himalayan belt, the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, parts of northern Bihar and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
options.C: Only coastal Kerala
options.D: Only Rajasthan

questions.explanation: The highest-hazard areas include much of the northeastern region, parts of the Himalayan belt, the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, parts of northern Bihar and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Exact boundaries should be checked on the applicable BIS seismic zoning map.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which areas are broadly associated with Zone IV?

options.A: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands only
options.B: Parts of the Himalayan and sub-Himalayan region, Delhi and other selected areas
options.C: Only the Rann of Kutch
options.D: Only peninsular India

questions.explanation: Parts of the Himalayan and sub-Himalayan region, Delhi and other selected areas fall in Zone IV. The exact pattern is map-specific and should be read from the official BIS map rather than inferred from state boundaries.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the approximate distribution of India's land area among seismic zones according to a Ministry of Earth Sciences parliamentary answer in 2022?

options.A: About 5% in Zone V, 10% in Zone IV, 20% in Zone III, and the rest in Zone II
options.B: About 11% in Zone V, 18% in Zone IV, 30% in Zone III and the remaining area in Zone II
options.C: About 25% in Zone V, 25% in Zone IV, 25% in Zone III, and 25% in Zone II
options.D: About 50% in Zone V and 50% in Zone IV

questions.explanation: A Ministry of Earth Sciences parliamentary answer in 2022 gave approximate figures of about 11% in Zone V, 18% in Zone IV, 30% in Zone III and the remaining area in Zone II. These are approximate area shares, not predictions of the probability of an earthquake in a particular year.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does a seismic zone tell the exact probability or date of an earthquake?

options.A: Yes, it predicts exactly when an earthquake will occur
options.B: No, seismic zoning is a planning classification of expected hazard, not a prediction of when or exactly where an earthquake will occur
options.C: Yes, it gives the exact probability for each year
options.D: It predicts the magnitude but not the date

questions.explanation: No. Seismic zoning is a planning classification of expected hazard, not a prediction of when or exactly where an earthquake will occur.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does every location within one seismic zone experience identical shaking?

options.A: Yes, all locations in a zone experience identical shaking
options.B: No, local soil, sediment thickness, topography, basin effects, fault proximity and building conditions can produce different levels of shaking within the same zone
options.C: Only in Zone V
options.D: Only in Zone II

questions.explanation: No. Local soil, sediment thickness, topography, basin effects, fault proximity and building conditions can produce different levels of shaking within the same zone.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which seismic zones cover Karnataka?

options.A: Zone IV and Zone V
options.B: Zone II and Zone III; there are no Zone IV or Zone V areas in the official district-wise summary cited by the Ministry of Earth Sciences
options.C: Zone I and Zone II
options.D: Zone V only

questions.explanation: Karnataka includes areas classified in Seismic Zone II and Zone III under the BIS seismic zoning map. There are no Zone IV or Zone V areas in the official district-wise summary cited by the Ministry of Earth Sciences.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which Karnataka districts are listed as having Zone III areas in the Ministry of Earth Sciences' 2022 parliamentary answer?

options.A: Kalaburagi, Bidar, Raichur, Koppal
options.B: Belagavi, Bagalkot, Vijayapura, Uttara Kannada, Shivamogga, Udupi, Chikkamagaluru, Bengaluru, Dakshina Kannada, Kodagu, Mysuru and Chamarajanagar
options.C: Gadag, Dharwad, Haveri, Ballari
options.D: Chitradurga, Davanagere, Tumakuru, Kolar

questions.explanation: The answer lists Belagavi, Bagalkot, Vijayapura, Uttara Kannada, Shivamogga, Udupi, Chikkamagaluru, Bengaluru (then listed as Bangalore), Dakshina Kannada, Kodagu, Mysuru and Chamarajanagar as containing Zone III areas, often alongside Zone II portions. Udupi is listed as Zone III.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which districts were listed as Zone II only in the 2022 MoES table?

options.A: Belagavi, Bagalkot, Vijayapura, Uttara Kannada
options.B: Kalaburagi, Bidar, Raichur, Koppal, Gadag, Dharwad, Haveri, Ballari, Chitradurga, Davanagere, Tumakuru, Kolar, Bengaluru Rural, Mandya and Hassan
options.C: Shivamogga, Udupi, Chikkamagaluru, Bengaluru
options.D: Dakshina Kannada, Kodagu, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar

questions.explanation: Kalaburagi (then Gulbarga), Bidar, Raichur, Koppal, Gadag, Dharwad, Haveri, Ballari (then Bellary), Chitradurga, Davanagere, Tumakuru (then Tumkur), Kolar, Bengaluru Rural, Mandya and Hassan were listed as Zone II in that table.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Is the entire district necessarily in one seismic zone in Karnataka?

options.A: Yes, each district is entirely in one zone
options.B: No, several districts are listed as spanning Zone II and Zone III; a district boundary does not necessarily coincide with a seismic-zone boundary
options.C: Only Belagavi spans two zones
options.D: Only coastal districts span two zones

questions.explanation: No. Several districts are listed as spanning Zone II and Zone III. A district boundary does not necessarily coincide with a seismic-zone boundary; the location of a specific town or site should be checked against the official map.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which parts of Karnataka deserve particular attention in earthquake risk planning?

options.A: Only the eastern districts
options.B: The 2022 MoES table identifies Zone III portions in several districts, including parts of northern Karnataka, the western coastal belt and the southern/western districts
options.C: Only Bengaluru
options.D: Only the northern districts

questions.explanation: The 2022 MoES table identifies Zone III portions in several districts, including parts of northern Karnataka, the western coastal belt and the southern/western districts. Local hazard also depends on geology, site conditions and the vulnerability of buildings.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the role of KSNDMC in Karnataka?

options.A: It conducts elections in Karnataka
options.B: It is the Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre, the state's nodal agency for monitoring seismic activity with a network of permanent seismic monitoring stations across Karnataka
options.C: It builds earthquake-resistant buildings
options.D: It issues tsunami warnings for India

questions.explanation: The Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC) is the state's nodal agency for monitoring seismic activity. Its published geological-hazard information describes a network of permanent seismic monitoring stations across Karnataka.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does a lower seismic zone mean Karnataka is earthquake-free?

options.A: Yes, Zone II means no earthquakes can occur
options.B: No, earthquakes can occur in Zone II as well as Zone III; the classification indicates relative design hazard, not zero risk
options.C: Only Zone III can experience earthquakes
options.D: Karnataka has never experienced an earthquake

questions.explanation: No. Earthquakes can occur in Zone II as well as Zone III. The classification indicates relative design hazard, not zero risk.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a tsunami?

options.A: An ordinary wind-generated ocean wave
options.B: A series of long-period ocean waves generated by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water, which may travel across an ocean basin and produce severe coastal inundation when it reaches shallow water
options.C: A type of seismic wave that travels through the Earth
options.D: A tidal wave caused by the moon's gravity

questions.explanation: A tsunami is a series of long-period ocean waves generated by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water. It may travel across an ocean basin and produce severe coastal inundation when it reaches shallow water.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Is a tsunami the same as an ordinary sea wave?

options.A: Yes, they are identical
options.B: No, ordinary wind-generated waves mainly affect the ocean surface and have much shorter wavelengths; a tsunami involves the movement of a large water column, has a very long wavelength and period, and can travel across ocean basins
options.C: Yes, but tsunamis are larger
options.D: No, tsunamis are caused by wind

questions.explanation: No. Ordinary wind-generated waves mainly affect the ocean surface and have much shorter wavelengths. A tsunami involves the movement of a large water column, has a very long wavelength and period, and can travel across ocean basins.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can a tsunami consist of more than one wave?

options.A: No, a tsunami is a single wave
options.B: Yes, a tsunami is usually a series of waves; the first wave may not be the largest, and dangerous currents can continue for hours
options.C: Only in the Pacific Ocean
options.D: Only if caused by a volcanic eruption

questions.explanation: Yes. A tsunami is usually a series of waves. The first wave may not be the largest, and dangerous currents can continue for hours.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why can a tsunami be difficult to notice in deep ocean water?

options.A: Because it travels very slowly
options.B: Because in deep water, tsunami waves may have low wave height but very long wavelengths and travel at high speeds; their height increases as they enter shallow coastal waters and slow down
options.C: Because it only occurs at night
options.D: Because it is invisible in deep water

questions.explanation: In deep water, tsunami waves may have low wave height but very long wavelengths and travel at high speeds. Their height increases as they enter shallow coastal waters and slow down.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is run-up in the context of tsunamis?

options.A: The horizontal penetration of tsunami water inland from the shoreline
options.B: The maximum vertical height reached by tsunami water above a reference sea level on land
options.C: The speed at which a tsunami travels
options.D: The time between successive tsunami waves

questions.explanation: Run-up is the maximum vertical height reached by tsunami water above a reference sea level on land.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is inundation in the context of tsunamis?

options.A: The maximum vertical height reached by tsunami water
options.B: The horizontal penetration of tsunami water inland from the shoreline
options.C: The speed of tsunami waves in deep water
options.D: The warning system for tsunamis

questions.explanation: Inundation is the horizontal penetration of tsunami water inland from the shoreline.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the most common cause of destructive tsunamis?

options.A: Ordinary wind waves
options.B: Large, shallow undersea earthquakes that cause significant vertical displacement of the seabed
options.C: Daily tides
options.D: River floods

questions.explanation: Large, shallow undersea earthquakes that cause significant vertical displacement of the seabed are the most common cause of major destructive tsunamis.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does an undersea earthquake generate a tsunami?

options.A: By creating strong winds over the ocean
options.B: If a large earthquake suddenly lifts or drops the seabed, it displaces the overlying water column; the disturbance generates waves that radiate outward across the ocean
options.C: By heating the ocean water
options.D: By causing the moon's gravitational pull to increase

questions.explanation: If a large earthquake suddenly lifts or drops the seabed, it displaces the overlying water column. The disturbance generates waves that radiate outward across the ocean.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can all undersea earthquakes generate tsunamis?

options.A: Yes, every undersea earthquake generates a tsunami
options.B: No, many are too small, too deep, or produce mostly horizontal displacement; tsunami generation is especially associated with large shallow earthquakes that cause substantial vertical seabed movement
options.C: Only those with magnitude above 5
options.D: Only those in the Pacific Ocean

questions.explanation: No. Many are too small, too deep, or produce mostly horizontal displacement. Tsunami generation is especially associated with large shallow earthquakes that cause substantial vertical seabed movement.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can volcanic eruptions generate tsunamis?

options.A: No, only earthquakes can generate tsunamis
options.B: Yes, submarine or coastal volcanic eruptions, volcanic flank collapse, caldera collapse and pyroclastic flows entering the sea can displace water and generate tsunamis
options.C: Only if the volcano is underwater
options.D: Only in the Atlantic Ocean

questions.explanation: Yes. Submarine or coastal volcanic eruptions, volcanic flank collapse, caldera collapse and pyroclastic flows entering the sea can displace water and generate tsunamis.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can landslides generate tsunamis?

options.A: No, landslides cannot generate tsunamis
options.B: Yes, submarine landslides or large landslides entering a water body can displace water and generate local or regional tsunamis
options.C: Only if the landslide is very small
options.D: Only in lakes, not oceans

questions.explanation: Yes. Submarine landslides or large landslides entering a water body can displace water and generate local or regional tsunamis.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can meteorite impacts generate tsunamis?

options.A: No, meteorites cannot generate tsunamis
options.B: In principle, a large extraterrestrial impact into an ocean can displace water and generate tsunami waves, but such events are extremely rare
options.C: Yes, and they are very common
options.D: Only if the meteorite is small

questions.explanation: In principle, a large extraterrestrial impact into an ocean can displace water and generate tsunami waves, but such events are extremely rare.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does a submarine or coastal landslide displace water to generate a tsunami?

options.A: By heating the ocean water
options.B: A large mass moves into or beneath water, displacing water and can produce very large local waves
options.C: By creating strong winds
options.D: By changing the moon's gravity

questions.explanation: A submarine or coastal landslide involves a large mass moving into or beneath water, which displaces water and can produce very large local waves.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How can volcanic activity generate a tsunami?

options.A: Only by creating wind
options.B: Through explosion, collapse or material entering water, which displaces water and may generate local or regional tsunamis
options.C: Only by heating the ocean
options.D: Only by changing sea level

questions.explanation: Volcanic activity can generate tsunamis through explosion, collapse or material entering water, which displaces water and may generate local or regional tsunamis.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are the major effects of tsunamis?

options.A: Only coastal flooding
options.B: Coastal flooding and inundation, strong currents, drowning, injuries and deaths, destruction of buildings and infrastructure, erosion, saltwater contamination of soil and freshwater, damage to ports and fisheries, displacement of communities and economic disruption
options.C: Only damage to buildings
options.D: Only saltwater contamination

questions.explanation: Major effects include coastal flooding and inundation, strong currents, drowning, injuries and deaths, destruction of buildings and infrastructure, erosion, saltwater contamination of soil and freshwater, damage to ports and fisheries, displacement of communities and economic disruption.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How can tsunamis affect agriculture?

options.A: They have no effect on agriculture
options.B: Saltwater can contaminate fields and groundwater, damage crops, reduce soil productivity and harm livestock
options.C: They only affect fishing, not farming
options.D: They improve soil fertility

questions.explanation: Saltwater can contaminate fields and groundwater, damage crops, reduce soil productivity and harm livestock.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How can tsunamis affect the environment?

options.A: They have no environmental impact
options.B: They can erode beaches and dunes, move large amounts of sediment, damage mangroves and coastal habitats, spread debris and pollutants, and alter coastal ecosystems
options.C: They only affect marine life
options.D: They only cause temporary changes

questions.explanation: They can erode beaches and dunes, move large amounts of sediment, damage mangroves and coastal habitats, spread debris and pollutants, and alter coastal ecosystems.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why are ports and coastal infrastructure vulnerable to tsunamis?

options.A: Because they are built on weak soil
options.B: Powerful currents, debris impact, flooding and rapid water-level changes can damage ships, harbours, roads, bridges, railways, power systems and communication networks
options.C: Because they are always located in earthquake zones
options.D: Because they lack warning systems

questions.explanation: Powerful currents, debris impact, flooding and rapid water-level changes can damage ships, harbours, roads, bridges, railways, power systems and communication networks.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can a tsunami cause damage far inland?

options.A: No, tsunamis only affect the immediate coastline
options.B: Yes, the inland reach depends on wave characteristics and coastal topography; low-lying coastal plains, river mouths and bays may allow water to penetrate considerable distances
options.C: Only if the tsunami is very small
options.D: Only in the Pacific Ocean

questions.explanation: Yes. The inland reach depends on wave characteristics and coastal topography. Low-lying coastal plains, river mouths and bays may allow water to penetrate considerable distances.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why is the first tsunami wave not necessarily the largest?

options.A: Because the first wave always loses energy
options.B: A tsunami is a wave train whose waves interact with ocean-basin and coastal geometry; later waves can be larger or produce stronger currents than the first
options.C: Because the first wave is always the largest
options.D: Because later waves are always smaller

questions.explanation: A tsunami is a wave train whose waves interact with ocean-basin and coastal geometry. Later waves can be larger or produce stronger currents than the first.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What was the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami?

options.A: A tsunami caused by a volcanic eruption in Indonesia
options.B: A devastating tsunami generated by the great undersea earthquake off northern Sumatra on 26 December 2004, affecting many countries around the Indian Ocean including India's east coast and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
options.C: A tsunami caused by a landslide in Sri Lanka
options.D: A tsunami caused by a meteorite impact

questions.explanation: A devastating tsunami generated by the great undersea earthquake off northern Sumatra on 26 December 2004. It affected many countries around the Indian Ocean, including India's east coast and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which parts of India were severely affected by the 2004 tsunami?

options.A: Only the west coast
options.B: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands and parts of India's eastern coastline, including Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and the Union Territory of Puducherry
options.C: Only Gujarat
options.D: Only Mumbai

questions.explanation: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands and parts of India's eastern coastline, including Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and the Union Territory of Puducherry, were affected, with impacts varying by location.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can the west coast of India experience a tsunami?

options.A: No, only the east coast is at risk
options.B: Yes, although exposure differs from the east coast, the west coast is not immune to tsunami hazards; tsunami risk depends on the location and characteristics of the generating event and the propagation path
options.C: Only if the tsunami originates in the Arabian Sea
options.D: Only during the monsoon season

questions.explanation: Yes. Although exposure differs from the east coast, the west coast is not immune to tsunami hazards. Tsunami risk depends on the location and characteristics of the generating event and the propagation path.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are natural warning signs of a possible tsunami?

options.A: Clear skies and calm weather
options.B: A strong or long-lasting coastal earthquake, an unusual rapid rise or fall of sea level, and a loud ocean roar
options.C: Heavy rainfall and strong winds
options.D: A sudden drop in temperature

questions.explanation: A strong or long-lasting coastal earthquake, an unusual rapid rise or fall of sea level, and a loud ocean roar can be natural warning signs. People near the coast should move immediately to higher ground or inland if these signs occur.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Should people wait for an official warning after a strong coastal earthquake?

options.A: Yes, always wait for an official warning
options.B: No, if a person is in a coastal area and experiences strong or prolonged earthquake shaking, they should move immediately to higher ground or inland when safe to do so; do not wait for an official alert
options.C: Only wait if the earthquake is above magnitude 7
options.D: Only wait during the night

questions.explanation: No. If a person is in a coastal area and experiences strong or prolonged earthquake shaking, they should move immediately to higher ground or inland when safe to do so. Do not wait for an official alert.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is India's tsunami warning system?

options.A: Operated by the India Meteorological Department
options.B: India's tsunami early-warning capability is operated by the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), which monitors seismic information, sea-level observations and other data to issue tsunami advisories for the Indian Ocean region
options.C: Operated by the National Disaster Management Authority
options.D: Operated by the Indian Navy

questions.explanation: India's tsunami early-warning capability is operated by the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), which monitors seismic information, sea-level observations and other data to issue tsunami advisories for the Indian Ocean region.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does a tsunami warning mean the danger is over after the first wave?

options.A: Yes, the danger ends after the first wave
options.B: No, a tsunami consists of multiple waves and strong currents may persist; people should remain in safe locations until the competent authority officially declares the threat over
options.C: Only if the first wave was large
options.D: Only in the Pacific Ocean

questions.explanation: No. A tsunami consists of multiple waves and strong currents may persist. People should remain in safe locations until the competent authority officially declares the threat over.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How should households prepare before an earthquake?

options.A: Only stock food and water
options.B: Secure heavy furniture and appliances; keep heavy objects on lower shelves; identify safe places; practise Drop, Cover and Hold On; prepare an emergency kit; know how to shut off gas, electricity and water if safe; maintain family communication and meeting plans; and ensure buildings follow applicable earthquake-resistant standards
options.C: Only learn first aid
options.D: Only buy a fire extinguisher

questions.explanation: Secure heavy furniture and appliances; keep heavy objects on lower shelves; identify safe places; practise Drop, Cover and Hold On; prepare an emergency kit; know how to shut off gas, electricity and water if safe; maintain family communication and meeting plans; and ensure buildings follow applicable earthquake-resistant standards.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should an emergency kit for earthquake preparedness contain?

options.A: Only food and water
options.B: Drinking water, non-perishable food, torch, batteries, radio or charged power bank, first-aid supplies, essential medicines, whistle and copies of important documents
options.C: Only a first-aid kit
options.D: Only a torch and batteries

questions.explanation: Keep an emergency kit with drinking water, non-perishable food, torch, batteries, radio or charged power bank, first-aid supplies, essential medicines, whistle and copies of important documents.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should a person do during an earthquake indoors?

options.A: Run outside immediately
options.B: Drop, Cover and Hold On: Drop to hands and knees; take cover under a sturdy table or desk if available; protect the head and neck; hold on to the shelter until shaking stops; stay away from windows, glass, exterior walls and heavy objects; do not run outside while the building is shaking
options.C: Stand in a doorway
options.D: Use the elevator to evacuate

questions.explanation: Drop, Cover and Hold On. Drop to hands and knees; take cover under a sturdy table or desk if available; protect the head and neck; hold on to the shelter until shaking stops. Stay away from windows, glass, exterior walls and heavy objects. Do not run outside while the building is shaking.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should a person do if no sturdy table or desk is available during an earthquake?

options.A: Run outside immediately
options.B: Drop near an interior wall or low, stable furniture if appropriate, protect the head and neck with the arms, and stay away from windows and objects that could fall; avoid lifts and stairways during shaking
options.C: Stand in the center of the room
options.D: Lie flat on the floor

questions.explanation: Drop near an interior wall or low, stable furniture if appropriate, protect the head and neck with the arms, and stay away from windows and objects that could fall. Avoid lifts and stairways during shaking.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should a person do outdoors during an earthquake?

options.A: Stand near a building for protection
options.B: Move to an open area away from buildings, boundary walls, trees, streetlights, poles and overhead wires; stay there until the shaking stops
options.C: Lie down on the ground
options.D: Run towards the nearest tree

questions.explanation: Move to an open area away from buildings, boundary walls, trees, streetlights, poles and overhead wires. Stay there until the shaking stops.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should a person do while driving during an earthquake?

options.A: Speed up to get away quickly
options.B: Pull over carefully in a safe location away from bridges, flyovers, buildings, trees and power lines; stop, remain in the vehicle until shaking stops, and then proceed cautiously while watching for road damage
options.C: Stop immediately in the middle of the road
options.D: Get out of the vehicle and run

questions.explanation: Pull over carefully in a safe location away from bridges, flyovers, buildings, trees and power lines. Stop, remain in the vehicle until shaking stops, and then proceed cautiously while watching for road damage.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Should people use lifts during an earthquake?

options.A: Yes, lifts are the safest way to evacuate
options.B: No, do not use elevators during shaking or immediately after an earthquake; use stairs only after shaking stops and when the route is safe
options.C: Only if the building is tall
options.D: Only if the lift is modern

questions.explanation: No. Do not use elevators during shaking or immediately after an earthquake. Use stairs only after shaking stops and when the route is safe.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should people do immediately after an earthquake?

options.A: Return to damaged buildings to retrieve belongings
options.B: Expect aftershocks; check for injuries and provide first aid if safe; evacuate damaged buildings carefully; avoid damaged structures; check for gas leaks, fire and electrical hazards; follow official information; and avoid entering unsafe buildings
options.C: Use elevators to evacuate
options.D: Light candles to check for damage

questions.explanation: Expect aftershocks; check for injuries and provide first aid if safe; evacuate damaged buildings carefully; avoid damaged structures; check for gas leaks, fire and electrical hazards; follow official information; and avoid entering unsafe buildings.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should be done if a gas leak is suspected after an earthquake?

options.A: Light a match to check
options.B: Avoid flames and electrical switches; leave the area and report the leak; shut off the supply only if it is safe and you know how
options.C: Turn on all electrical switches
options.D: Ignore it and stay indoors

questions.explanation: If gas is suspected, avoid flames and electrical switches; leave the area and report the leak. Shut off the supply only if it is safe and you know how.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should people do about communication after an earthquake?

options.A: Make as many voice calls as possible
options.B: Use text messages where possible to reduce congestion on voice networks
options.C: Avoid all communication
options.D: Only use social media

questions.explanation: Use text messages where possible to reduce congestion on voice networks.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What should people near the coast do after a strong or long earthquake?

options.A: Wait for an official tsunami warning
options.B: Move to higher ground and follow tsunami evacuation instructions
options.C: Go to the beach to observe the ocean
options.D: Stay indoors

questions.explanation: If near the coast after a strong or long earthquake, move to higher ground and follow tsunami evacuation instructions.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is earthquake-resistant construction?

options.A: Construction that prevents all earthquake damage
options.B: The design and construction of buildings and infrastructure to resist expected earthquake forces without unacceptable collapse or loss of life, aiming to improve structural strength, ductility, connections and overall performance
options.C: Construction that only uses wood
options.D: Construction that ignores building codes

questions.explanation: It is the design and construction of buildings and infrastructure to resist expected earthquake forces without unacceptable collapse or loss of life. It aims to improve structural strength, ductility, connections and overall performance.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is ductility in earthquake engineering?

options.A: The ability of a material to conduct electricity
options.B: The ability of a material or structural system to undergo significant deformation beyond its elastic limit without sudden failure; ductile detailing helps structures dissipate earthquake energy
options.C: The ability of a building to float
options.D: The stiffness of a building

questions.explanation: Ductility is the ability of a material or structural system to undergo significant deformation beyond its elastic limit without sudden failure. Ductile detailing helps structures dissipate earthquake energy.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why is building-code compliance important for earthquake safety?

options.A: It is only a legal requirement with no safety benefit
options.B: Building codes provide engineering requirements for design, materials, detailing and construction according to seismic hazard; proper implementation reduces collapse risk and protects life
options.C: It only applies to tall buildings

questions.subject: General Knowledge

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can an earthquake be predicted accurately?

options.A: Yes, scientists can predict the exact date, location and magnitude
options.B: No, scientists can estimate seismic hazard and probabilities over time, monitor earthquakes and issue alerts after an earthquake has begun, but they cannot reliably predict the exact date, location and magnitude of a future earthquake
options.C: Yes, but only for shallow earthquakes
options.D: Only volcanic earthquakes can be predicted

questions.explanation: No. Scientists can estimate seismic hazard and probabilities over time, monitor earthquakes and issue alerts after an earthquake has begun, but they cannot reliably predict the exact date, location and magnitude of a future earthquake.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is an earthquake early-warning system?

options.A: A system that predicts earthquakes weeks in advance
options.B: It detects the faster-arriving seismic waves near an earthquake source and sends alerts that may reach more distant locations before stronger shaking arrives; it provides seconds to tens of seconds in some situations, not long-term prediction, and may not provide warning close to the epicentre
options.C: A system that prevents earthquakes from occurring
options.D: A system that only works for tsunamis

questions.explanation: It detects the faster-arriving seismic waves near an earthquake source and sends alerts that may reach more distant locations before stronger shaking arrives. questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Explain the causes of earthquakes and the elastic rebound theory. Which option best describes this?

options.A: Earthquakes are caused by wind; elastic rebound theory states that rocks bounce back after rain
options.B: Most earthquakes are tectonic, caused by sudden fault slip after stress accumulates; elastic rebound theory explains that rocks on either side of a locked fault gradually deform as tectonic stress builds, and when the fault ruptures, the rocks spring partly back towards an undeformed state, releasing stored energy
options.C: Earthquakes are caused by volcanic eruptions only; elastic rebound theory explains volcanic activity
options.D: Earthquakes are caused by ocean tides; elastic rebound theory explains tidal forces

questions.explanation: Most earthquakes are tectonic, caused by sudden fault slip after stress accumulates. Elastic rebound theory explains that rocks on either side of a locked fault gradually deform as tectonic stress builds. When the fault ruptures, the rocks spring partly back towards an undeformed state, releasing stored energy and generating an earthquake.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Differentiate focus and epicentre. Which option is correct?

options.A: Focus is on the surface; epicentre is inside the Earth
options.B: Focus is the point inside the Earth where rupture begins; epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface vertically above the focus
options.C: Both are the same point
options.D: Focus is the area of maximum damage; epicentre is the area of minimum damage

questions.explanation: Focus (hypocentre) is the point inside the Earth where the rupture begins and seismic energy is first released. Epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface vertically above the earthquake focus.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Describe P-waves, S-waves and surface waves. Which option is correct?

options.A: P-waves are shear waves traveling through solids only; S-waves are compressional and travel through all mediums; surface waves travel through the interior
options.B: P-waves are primary compressional waves traveling through solids, liquids and gases; S-waves are secondary shear waves traveling through solids only; surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) travel along the surface and often cause strong damage
options.C: P-waves and S-waves are both surface waves; Love and Rayleigh waves are body waves
options.D: All seismic waves travel at the same speed

questions.explanation: P-waves are primary or compressional seismic waves; they are the fastest and can travel through solids, liquids and gases. S-waves are secondary or shear seismic waves; they are slower than P-waves and cannot propagate through liquids. Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) travel along the Earth's surface and can produce large-amplitude shaking and substantial damage.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Differentiate Richter magnitude, moment magnitude and Mercalli intensity. Which option is correct?

options.A: All three measure the same thing
options.B: Richter magnitude is a local magnitude scale based on recorded wave amplitudes; moment magnitude is based on seismic moment and preferred for large earthquakes; Mercalli intensity describes observed shaking and damage at a location and varies from place to place
options.C: Richter magnitude measures intensity; Mercalli measures magnitude; moment magnitude measures depth
options.D: Moment magnitude measures observed damage; Richter measures seismic moment; Mercalli measures energy

questions.explanation: Richter magnitude (local magnitude) is based on recorded seismic-wave amplitudes. Moment magnitude is based on seismic moment and is preferred for large earthquakes. Mercalli intensity describes observed shaking and damage at a particular location and varies from place to place.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Explain India's seismic zones and identify the highest-risk zone. Which option is correct?

options.A: India has three zones: I, II and III; Zone I is highest risk
options.B: India's commonly cited BIS framework has four zones: II, III, IV and V; Zone V is the highest seismic-hazard zone, including much of the northeast, parts of the Himalayan belt, the Rann of Kutch, parts of northern Bihar and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
options.C: India has five zones: I to V; Zone III is highest risk
options.D: India has two zones: II and III; Zone II is highest risk

questions.explanation: The BIS seismic zoning framework in IS 1893 (Part 1): 2016 classifies India into four zones: Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV and Zone V. Zone V is the highest seismic-hazard zone; it includes much of the northeastern region, parts of the Himalayan belt, the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat, parts of northern Bihar and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Describe the seismic zones and earthquake-monitoring arrangements of Karnataka. Which option is correct?
